gloss: To cover something with a protective layer of metal or other hard material.
examples: The company *armors* trucks for use in war zones.
They *armored* the embassy doors after the attack.
Every vehicle in the convoy has been *armored*.
contrast: American English spells it *armor, armored, armoring*; British English writes *armour, armoured, armouring*.

gloss: To stir up a feeling or reaction in someone.
examples: Questions like that *arouse* suspicion immediately.
His sudden wealth *aroused* the interest of the tax office.
The story has *aroused* strong feelings on both sides.
contrast: Do not confuse *arouse*, which is regular (*aroused, aroused*), with *arise*, which is irregular (*arose, arisen*).

ru: предъявлять обвинение в суде, привлекать к суду
gloss: To bring someone before a court to hear the charges and answer them.
examples: Prosecutors will *arraign* the suspect on Monday morning.
She was *arraigned* on three counts of fraud.
The court has *arraigned* all four defendants.
contrast: The *g* is silent: *arraign* is uh-RAYN. You are *arraigned* **on** a charge.

gloss: To find something out for certain by checking the facts.
examples: We need to *ascertain* who was in the building that night.
Investigators *ascertained* the cause of the fire within a week.
The police have not yet *ascertained* how the thieves got in.

transitivity: both — transitive (the fumes *asphyxiated* two workers), intransitive (the miners *asphyxiated* underground)
gloss: To kill or be killed by a lack of oxygen.
examples: Carbon monoxide can *asphyxiate* a person in minutes.
Two workers were *asphyxiated* by fumes inside the tank.
The gas was slowly *asphyxiating* everyone in the basement.

gloss: To have a strong desire to reach something important.
examples: Many of these students *aspire* to a career in medicine.
She *aspired* to be the first in her family to finish college.
He has always *aspired* to something bigger than this town.
contrast: *aspire* takes **to**: *aspire to a position*, *aspire to be something*. Never "aspire for".

gloss: To attack someone or something violently, with blows or with words.
examples: Critics *assail* the mayor every time the budget comes up.
Reporters *assailed* the senator with questions about the leak.
The coast has been *assailed* by three storms this month.

gloss: To state something firmly as true, or to claim a right with confidence.
examples: The report *asserts* that the numbers were changed on purpose.
She *asserted* her right to speak to a lawyer.
He has *asserted* his innocence from the very first day.

transitivity: both — transitive (*assimilate* new information), intransitive (the family *assimilated* quickly)
gloss: To take something in and absorb it fully, or to become part of a larger group.
examples: It takes weeks to *assimilate* this much new material.
Her grandparents *assimilated* within a few years of arriving.
The team is still *assimilating* the data from last season.

gloss: To shock someone with surprise or amazement.
examples: The size of the crowd will *astound* you.
His answer *astounded* the whole committee.
We were *astounded* by how quickly the work was finished.

gloss: To make up for something wrong that you have done.
examples: Nothing he does now can *atone* for that decision.
She *atoned* for the mistake by working through the weekend.
He has spent years *atoning* for the harm he caused.
contrast: *atone* takes **for**: *atone for a mistake*, never "atone a mistake".

transitivity: both — transitive (weeks in bed *atrophy* the muscles), intransitive (the muscles *atrophy*)
gloss: To waste away and grow weak from lack of use.
examples: Muscles *atrophy* quickly when a leg is in a cast.
His Russian *atrophied* after ten years away from home.
The program has *atrophied* since the funding was cut.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *atrophies, atrophied*, but the *-ing* form keeps it: *atrophying*.

gloss: To make someone or something sensitive and well adjusted to something.
examples: Years in the classroom *attune* a teacher to small changes in mood.
The training *attuned* the staff to the needs of older customers.
She is well *attuned* to what her readers want.
contrast: Almost always used with **to**: *attuned to the market*. American English says uh-TOON, not "uh-TYOON".

gloss: To make something larger or stronger by adding to it.
examples: Many teachers *augment* their income with summer work.
The city *augmented* the police budget after the vote.
The library has *augmented* its collection with three thousand new titles.

transitivity: both — transitive (the result *augurs* a difficult year), intransitive (this *augurs* well for the talks)
gloss: To be a sign of how something is going to turn out.
examples: Weak sales *augur* badly for the holiday season.
The early numbers *augured* well for the new director.
Nothing in that first meeting *augured* the trouble that followed.
contrast: Do not confuse *augur*, to foretell, with *auger*, a tool for drilling holes; both are said AW-gur.

gloss: To write a book, a report, or a piece of legislation.
examples: Two economists *author* the annual report together.
She *authored* the bill that became law last spring.
He has *authored* more than a dozen novels.

transitivity: both — transitive (the phone *autocorrected* my message), intransitive (the field *autocorrects* as you type)
gloss: To change a typed word automatically to the one the software thinks you meant.
examples: My phone always *autocorrects* his name to something else.
The app *autocorrected* "definitely" to "defiantly".
I sent the text without noticing that it had *autocorrected* the address.

gloss: To wait for something that is expected.
examples: Three more patients *await* their test results.
We *awaited* the verdict in complete silence.
He is *awaiting* trial in a county jail.
contrast: *await* takes a direct object with no preposition: *await a decision*, but *wait **for** a decision*.

transitivity: both — transitive (the noise *awakened* the baby), intransitive (she *awakened* at dawn)
gloss: To wake up, or to wake someone else up, used of feelings as well as of sleep.
examples: One phone call can *awaken* the whole house.
The smell of coffee *awakened* something like hope in him.
She had *awakened* long before the alarm went off.
contrast: *awaken* is regular: *awakened, awakened*. It is *awake* that is irregular: *awoke, awoken*.

gloss: To fill someone with a feeling of wonder and deep respect.
examples: The scale of the canyon *awes* almost every visitor.
We were *awed* by the silence inside the cathedral.
Her performance has *awed* critics across the country.
contrast: The silent *e* drops before *-ing*: *awe → awing*.

gloss: To get rid of something suddenly, such as a job, a show, or a budget line.
examples: The network may *axe* the show after one season.
The company *axed* four hundred jobs in a single morning.
Three of the projects have already been *axed*.
contrast: American English also spells it *ax*; both spellings give *axed* and *axing*.

gloss: To talk quickly and foolishly, or to make a soft running sound like a stream.
examples: The twins *babble* to each other for hours.
He *babbled* something about missing his flight.
A little stream was *babbling* just beyond the trees.

ru: нянчиться, баловать, обращаться как с ребёнком
gloss: To treat someone with far too much care and protection.
examples: Don't *baby* him — he can carry his own bag.
His mother *babied* him well into his twenties.
You are *babying* that car; it will be fine on gravel.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *babies, babied*, but the *-ing* form keeps it: *babying*.

gloss: To put an earlier date on a document or a payment than the real one.
examples: The contract lets the company *backdate* the raise to January.
Someone had *backdated* the invoices by six months.
Executives were accused of *backdating* their stock options.

gloss: To produce the opposite of the result that was intended.
examples: Threats like that usually *backfire*.
The ad campaign *backfired* badly.
Their attempt to bury the story has *backfired* on them.

ru: идти на попятную, отступать от сказанного; возвращаться тем же путём
gloss: To go back the way you came, or to take back something you said earlier.
examples: Let me *backtrack* a little and explain that first step again.
The governor *backtracked* within hours of the interview.
He has been *backtracking* on that promise all week.

gloss: To put food on a hook or in a trap, or to provoke someone on purpose.
examples: He *baits* the hook with a piece of shrimp.
She *baited* her brother until he lost his temper.
The traps had been *baited* the night before.
contrast: Do not confuse *bait* with *bate*, which survives only in the phrase *with bated breath*.

gloss: To refuse suddenly to do or accept something.
examples: Buyers *balk* at prices like that.
The board *balked* when it saw the final figure.
He is *balking* at signing anything before his lawyer reads it.
contrast: *balk* takes **at**: *balk at the cost*. British English spells it *baulk*, and the *l* is silent either way: BAWK.

gloss: To grow very quickly to a much larger size.
examples: Repair costs can *balloon* once the walls are opened up.
The deficit *ballooned* during the crisis.
Class sizes have *ballooned* since the two schools merged.

gloss: To trick or thoroughly confuse someone, usually in order to get something.
examples: Salesmen like that *bamboozle* people every day.
He *bamboozled* his neighbors into lending him money.
We were completely *bamboozled* by the paperwork.

transitivity: both — transitive (he *banged* the door), intransitive (someone was *banging* on the wall)
gloss: To hit something hard, making a loud noise.
examples: Please don't *bang* the door when you leave.
She *banged* her knee on the table leg.
Someone has been *banging* on the pipes all morning.

gloss: To send someone away from a place as a punishment, or to drive a thought out of your mind.
examples: Old kings could *banish* anyone who displeased them.
He was *banished* from the country for twenty years.
She spent the whole flight *banishing* thoughts of the meeting.
contrast: Ends in *-sh*, so the third person adds *-es*: *banishes*.

ru: класть в банк, держать деньги в банке
transitivity: both — transitive (she *banked* the check), intransitive (we *bank* at a credit union)
gloss: To put or keep money in a bank.
examples: Where do you *bank*?
He *banked* most of the prize money.
They have *banked* with the same branch for thirty years.

gloss: To leave a person or company with no money at all.
examples: One bad season can *bankrupt* a small farm.
The lawsuit nearly *bankrupted* the family.
Medical bills have *bankrupted* thousands of households.

gloss: To admit someone into the Christian church in a ceremony using water.
examples: The priest will *baptize* the child on Sunday.
She was *baptized* in the same church as her mother.
He has *baptized* three generations of that family.
contrast: American English spells it *baptize, baptized*; British English usually writes *baptise, baptised*.

gloss: To uncover something, or to reveal something private.
examples: The dog *bares* its teeth at strangers.
He *bared* his arm so the nurse could find a vein.
She has never *bared* that part of her life to anyone.
contrast: *bare* sounds exactly like *bear*, the animal and the irregular verb *bear, bore, borne*. The silent *e* drops before *-ing*: *baring*.

gloss: To block a road or a doorway with something heavy so that nobody can get through.
examples: Protesters *barricade* the main road every spring.
The gunman *barricaded* himself in the back office.
Both entrances had been *barricaded* with office furniture.

gloss: To work as a bartender, serving drinks in a bar.
examples: She *bartends* three nights a week to pay for school.
He *bartended* at a hotel downtown all summer.
I have been *bartending* since I was twenty-one.

gloss: To build something on a particular fact, idea, or place as its foundation.
examples: Scientists *base* that conclusion on thirty years of data.
The movie was *based* on a true story.
The company is *basing* its new office in Denver.
contrast: *base* takes **on**: *based on the evidence*. It sounds like *bass*, the low voice.

gloss: To hit something hard, or to attack someone harshly in words.
examples: Politicians *bash* each other for months before an election.
He *bashed* his elbow against the door frame.
The paper has been *bashing* the mayor all year.
contrast: Ends in *-sh*, so the third person adds *-es*: *bashes*.

transitivity: both — transitive (she *battled* cancer for years), intransitive (the two sides *battled* over the bill)
gloss: To fight or struggle hard against someone or something.
examples: Crews *battle* wildfires along the coast every August.
He *battled* the insurance company for eighteen months.
She has been *battling* a cold all week.

gloss: To cry or shout very loudly.
examples: Babies *bawl* when they are hungry.
She *bawled* through the whole ceremony.
He was *bawling* into the phone by the time I got there.
contrast: *bawl* sounds exactly like *ball*.

ru: вытаскивать на берег; выбрасываться на берег
transitivity: both — transitive (*beach* the canoe above the tide line), intransitive (three whales *beached* overnight)
gloss: To pull a boat up onto the shore, or of a sea animal, to become stranded on land.
examples: We usually *beach* the kayaks near the point.
A young whale *beached* south of the pier on Tuesday.
The ferry has been *beached* since the storm.
contrast: Ends in *-ch*, so the third person adds *-es*: *beaches*. It sounds like *beech*, the tree.

transitivity: both — transitive (they *beamed* the signal to the station), intransitive (she *beamed* at the news)
gloss: To smile broadly with happiness, or to send out light or a signal.
examples: The satellites *beam* the game to half the world.
She *beamed* when they called her name.
He was *beaming* all the way through the ceremony.

gloss: To make a place or a thing look more attractive.
examples: Volunteers *beautify* the park every spring.
The city *beautified* the waterfront ahead of the festival.
They have been *beautifying* the old train station for months.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *beautifies, beautified*, but the *-ing* form keeps it: *beautifying*.
